result.summary: Disgusted by the Propoetides, the sculptor Pygmalion stays unmarried and carves an ivory woman with whom he falls in love. At Venus's festival he prays for a wife like his statue, and the goddess brings the ivory to life. They marry and have a son, Paphos.

scenes.title: Pygmalion loves his ivory statue
scenes.summary: Repelled by women's vices, Pygmalion lives alone and carves a lovely ivory maiden. He falls in love with it, kissing, adorning and bedding it as if it were alive.
scenes.stakes: Pygmalion risks a hopeless, unreturned love for a lifeless object, and deception of his own senses.

scenes.title: Venus brings the statue to life
scenes.summary: At Venus's festival Pygmalion timidly prays for a wife like his ivory maid. Venus grants it, the statue warms into a living woman, and after their marriage she bears Paphos.
scenes.stakes: Pygmalion stands to lose his one hope of a beloved wife if the goddess refuses his prayer.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet linking Pygmalion to Paphos on Cyprus, a center of Venus's worship.

notable_quotes.reason: Captures the story's central idea of art so perfect it conceals itself.
Pygmalion's hesitant, indirect prayer, not daring to ask for the statue itself.

analysis.text: The tale explores desire, art and illusion: the artist's creation becomes so lifelike that love makes it real. It also follows Orpheus's songs of unusual loves.
Ovid's misogynistic framing reflects ancient views of women, though the story is told with playful sympathy for the lover.

legacy.text: The story inspired George Bernard Shaw's play Pygmalion (1913), and the psychological term 'Pygmalion effect'.
Shaw's play was adapted into the musical My Fair Lady (1956) and its 1964 film.

fun_facts.text: The name Galatea for the statue is not in Ovid; it was added by later writers.

language_notes.text: The Propœtides were women of Amathus in Cyprus who denied Venus's divinity and became the first prostitutes, then turned to stone, as told just before this passage.
The son is Paphos, from whom the island and city of Paphos in Cyprus were said to take their name.
The braces {so} and similar curly brackets mark words the translator added for clarity; they are not in the Latin.
Tears of the Heliades are amber: the daughters of the Sun (Helios) wept for their brother Phaethon and were turned into poplars whose tears hardened into amber.
Sidonian shell means Tyrian purple dye, made from murex shellfish at Sidon and Tyre, a costly luxury colour.
Heifers with gilded horns were typical sacrificial victims; the gilding and white coats marked them as fit offerings to the goddess.
Pygmalion's hedged wording, 'like to this statue,' avoids boldly asking for the statue itself, showing his fear of presumption.
The flame leaping up three times is a favourable omen; three was a lucky, ritual number.
Hymettian wax: honey-wax from Mount Hymettus near Athens, famed for its bees and honey.
Paphian: of Paphos, a Cyprus city sacred to Venus; here it means Cypriot.
The moon's horns gathered into a full orb nine times means nine lunar months, the length of pregnancy.

context_notes.text: Sentences 0 and 1 are the translator's summary headings, not Ovid's verse; the story proper begins in sentence 2.
The bracketed [40] is a footnote marker from the translator's edition, not part of the poem.
Venus, goddess of love, was strongly linked with Cyprus, where her cult was centred and where she was said to have come ashore.
Paphos, the son named here, gives his name to the Cyprian city of Paphos, a major centre of Venus's worship.

literary_notes.text: Art conceals art: the statue's skill is so great that it hides itself, making the work look like living nature.
Love is described as a flame in his breast, a common image of passion, here directed at a lifeless thing.
He tests whether it is flesh yet refuses to admit it is ivory, showing his self-deception.
His fears of bruising the limbs show obsessive tenderness and how fully he treats the statue as a living woman.
The list of gifts piles up small, girlish presents, conveying his devotion and the wooing of a real lover.
Softening ivory is compared to wax yielding to the fingers, making the miraculous change seem tangible and gradual.
The throbbing veins give tactile proof of life, settling Pygmalion's doubts and the reader's.
Her first sight of lover and sky marks a birth into the world, like waking.
